notes.meaning: God speaks with sharp irony, pretending Job is old enough to have been there when the universe was created. Since Job is merely a mortal born yesterday, he knows almost nothing about how the world began. This question humbles human pride by showing how tiny our lifespan is compared to the eternal Lord.

God asks Job if he has ever visited the hidden storehouses where snow and hail are kept. The Lord describes hail and severe weather as His reserve weapons, ready to be unleashed in times of distress, battle, and divine judgment. Human beings cannot produce these forces of nature or control when they strike.

The Lord asks Job if he knows the path along which daylight spreads or how the scorching east wind is scattered over the earth. Both the spreading rays of morning light and the sudden blast of desert winds operate far beyond human guidance. Only God determines their courses and directs where they go.

God asks who cuts channels through the sky for torrential rains and clears a highway for the thunderbolt. Rains and lightning do not fall in blind confusion, but follow the precise tracks God has prepared for them. No human being has the ability to steer a storm or guide where a lightning strike lands.

The Lord points out that He sends rain upon empty deserts where no human being lives to cultivate the soil. He faithfully waters this lonely wilderness so that fresh, tender grass can sprout for the wild animals living there. This demonstrates that God cares for His whole creation for its own sake, not just for human benefit.

God asks whether the rain has a human father or who brought forth the sparkling drops of dew. No person can invent moisture or command droplets of dew to appear on the morning grass. Rain and dew have no human maker, coming solely from the generous hand of the Creator.

God pictures ice and frost as though they were born from a mother's womb, asking who could produce such wonders. Under bitter cold, moving waters turn as hard as stone, and the entire surface of the deep lake freezes solid. This dramatic transformation from flowing water to rock-like ice displays God's extraordinary power over nature.

God points Job to the night sky, asking if he can tie the cluster of the Pleiades or loosen the belt of Orion. In ancient times, the Pleiades were associated with the arrival of warm spring flowers, while Orion marked the arrival of stormy winter. Man can neither hold back the joyful spring nor untie the freezing grip of winter.

The Lord asks if Job can guide the great constellations across the heavens or lead out the Bear and her cubs in their proper seasons. These massive star groups march across the night sky in perfect order throughout the year. God alone directs the movements of the cosmos while humans can only look up in reverence.

God asks Job if he understands the fixed rules that govern the starry heavens or if he can establish their rule over the earth. The Lord set up regular natural laws that keep the cosmos in orderly rhythm and affect life below. Because humans did not establish these laws and cannot alter them, we must trust the One who does.

The Lord challenges Job to call out to the clouds and order a flood of rain to pour down over his fields. A person can shout into the sky all day, but the clouds will never answer or drop a single shower at a human order. Rain falls only when the Lord commands the skies to open.

God asks if Job can send forth lightning bolts and have them report back like obedient servants saying, 'Here we are!' Flashes of lightning obey God instantly, striking only where He directs them. Human beings tremble before the fury of lightning and have no authority to give it orders.

God asks who gave wisdom to the human heart and planted understanding inside the human mind. The ability to think, observe, and reason about the world is entirely a gift from our Creator. It is foolish to use our God-given intelligence to question the perfect wisdom of the One who gave it to us.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the rare Hebrew words refer to creatures like the ibis and the rooster, known in ancient lore for predicting the Nile flood or sunrise, or to celestial phenomena like thunderbolts.

notes.meaning: God asks who possesses the wisdom to count the clouds or tip over the skies' water jars to pour down rain. During a severe drought, the dry ground bakes into a hard crust and clumps together into dusty lumps until rain softens it. Only God knows the right time to release moisture and renew the parched earth.

The Lord shifts Job's attention to the animal kingdom, asking if Job can hunt food for a lioness and satisfy the hunger of fierce young lions. These predators wait silently in their thickets and crouch deep inside their dens for an opportunity to feed. Even though wild lions are dangerous to humans, God faithfully provides their daily food in the wilderness.

The Lord asks who supplies food for the raven when its hungry chicks wander about and cry out to God. People often considered the raven an unpleasant and ill-omened bird, yet God hears its cries and feeds it. If God watches over even a small and despised bird, His children can be sure He will never forget their needs.
